escapeBrief:
Two players, never in the same room. The power has failed in the fog. One player is in the cellars with the water board (mechanical, so it works in the dark); the other is on the main floor with the electrical switchboard, which wakes once they restore the mains. Both boards measure the same eight rooms, each room's load on a rail, and both are the variance meter: between, within, and the share explained, with a red line at 35%.

Each board has the same eight room switches, so any grouping of the rooms can be set; the printed default groups them by wing, house against cellars. On electricity the wing clears the line (37%). On water it explains nothing (0%), while wet rooms against dry clear it (45%). Both players are right about their own board, and that is the trap: each obvious grouping is right for one utility and wrong for the building.

Exactly one grouping clears the line on both boards: the four rooms on the hidden service passage (library, laboratory, boiler room, archive vault), at 47% and 51%. The passage carries both the heating main and the heating cable, so those rooms draw more of both. Neither board points to it alone (15 and 17 groupings clear each line, and the passage tops neither), so the pair have to compare which groupings work on whose board. The passage door is a panel of the same eight switches; setting it to the passage rooms opens it, and that is the way out.

The echo is the interaction rung: the wing's effect depends on what you measure, and only a grouping that explains both holds.
title: Shut In
subtitle: Rothamsted Experimental Station, a foggy November morning in the late 1920s
story:
The staff have gone home for the long weekend and left the two of you to finish the report on the hay trial: forty-eight plots, each given a nitrogen dressing (none, nitrate of soda or sulphate of ammonia), lime or no lime, and minerals or none. The Director's draft rests on two averages: sulphate of ammonia makes the most hay, and sulphate of ammonia ruins a meadow. Test both. Work out how much of the difference between the plots each treatment explains, and where an average misleads.

A storm blew through in the night, and near dawn it brought the power line down. The caretaker locked the cellar stair on his way out, not knowing anyone was below, and took the key. One of you is shut in the cellars with a fading flashlight and the botanical survey: how many species grow on every plot. The other is on the main floor with the weighing book: the hay cut from every plot. You can call to each other through the floors, but you cannot see each other's pages, and you will not agree on what matters most. You are both right.

Somewhere in this house an old service passage joins the two floors, and nobody remembers its route. The building's switchboard and its water board can find it, but only if you read them together.

debrief.title: What you did
debrief.intro: This scenario was analysis of variance, run twice on the same hay trial: one of you weighed the hay, the other counted the species on the same forty-eight plots. You each measured how much of the variation one treatment explains on its own, ranked the three treatments by that share, then fitted two treatments together and read the interaction row first. In the last room each of you found that the dressing that looks best on average is not the best on one kind of ground, so the answer depended on where you looked and what you measured. Here is what you did.

musicCredit.text: Erik Satie, Gnossiennes 1-7, played by Thurzó Zoltán (Pianist On Road, YouTube)

done.title: The report is written
done.body: Your half of the report is done, and your partner's finding will not match yours. Neither of you has made a mistake: the dressing that looks best on average fails on one kind of ground, and which one depends on what you measured.

M.title: The report is written
M.body: Sulphate of ammonia does make the most hay on average, but on unlimed ground nitrate of soda beats it. Your half of the report is done. Your partner below has a different finding, and neither of you is wrong. Now find the passage.

C.title: The report is written
C.body: Sulphate of ammonia does leave the fewest species on average, but on limed ground it leaves the most. Your half of the report is done. Your partner above has a different finding, and neither of you is wrong. Now find the passage.

escapeDone.title: Through the wall
escapeDone.body: The panel takes your pattern on both sides of the passage. The library bookcase swings open above, the cellar door gives below, and you meet halfway up a narrow stair inside the wall, with the heating main and the cable running down beside you. The four rooms that drew more of both water and power were the four on this stair. Neither board could have shown it alone.

coverPrompt: Minimalist stylised thumbnail poster, square: the flat dark silhouette of an old gabled manor house with tall clustered chimneys, seen in cross-section like a doll's house, low fog lying in bands across its front; inside the thick wall between two rooms, one narrow stair climbs from a dark cellar to the floor above, and one warm amber glow from a single lamp halfway up the stair lights it. Bold, simple shapes that read at very small size, strong negative space. Flat limited palette: fog grey, soot black, old brick red and one warm amber glow. No people, no lettering, no text, no numbers, no border.
